questions.prompt: Using the Master Theorem, what is the solution of `T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n`?
questions.explanation: Here n^(log₂4) = n² and f(n) = n is polynomially smaller, so Case 1 applies and the leaves dominate.

questions.prompt: A binary counter starts at 0 and is incremented 8 times. How many bit flips occur in total, counting every 0→1 and 1→0 change?
questions.explanation: Bit 0 flips 8 times, bit 1 flips 4, bit 2 flips 2, bit 3 flips once: 8+4+2+1 = 15, less than 2n.

questions.prompt: Match each recurrence to its solution.
questions.explanation: Master Theorem Case 2, Case 2, Case 1, and Case 3 respectively.

questions.prompt: Merge the sorted halves [3, 5, 8] and [1, 4, 9] while counting inversions. How many cross-half inversions (a left element greater than a right element) are there?
Median of medians splits the input into groups of what size? Give the number.
questions.explanation: Groups of 5 make the recursion T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n), which solves to O(n).

questions.prompt: Write `count_inversions(nums)` that returns the number of pairs `i < j` with `nums[i] > nums[j]`.
questions.explanation: Count every out-of-order pair; merge sort does the same in O(n log n) but any correct count passes.

questions.prompt: Which data structure lets Kruskal's algorithm test quickly whether an edge would form a cycle?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's keeps components in a union-find; an edge is safe iff its endpoints have different roots.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Kruskal's algorithm in order.
items: Add it if its endpoints are in different components
Stop once V−1 edges have been chosen
questions.explanation: Kruskal's processes edges in sorted order, adding only those that join different components.

questions.prompt: Build a Huffman tree for frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13, 16, 45. What is the total weighted code length, the sum of frequency × code length over all symbols?
questions.explanation: The merges produce 14, 25, 30, 55, 100, and the weighted length equals the sum of merged weights: 14+25+30+55+100 = 224.

questions.prompt: What is the running time of Bellman-Ford on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges V−1 times.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms correctly compute shortest paths on a graph with negative edge weights but no negative cycle?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy choice and BFS both assume non-negative (or unit) weights.

questions.prompt: The value of a maximum s-t flow equals the capacity of a minimum s-t cut.
questions.explanation: This is the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the bitmask DP for the Traveling Salesman Problem on n cities?
questions.explanation: There are n·2ⁿ states and each does O(n) transitions.

questions.prompt: Matrices A (10×20), B (20×5), C (5×30) are multiplied. What is the minimum number of scalar multiplications over all parenthesizations?
Write `min_chain_cost(dims)` for matrix chain multiplication: matrix `i` has size `dims[i] × dims[i+1]`. Return the minimum number of scalar multiplications to multiply the whole chain.
questions.explanation: Interval DP: split the chain at k and add the cost of the final multiplication.

questions.prompt: What is the time for a range-sum query on a segment tree over n elements?
questions.explanation: A query combines O(log n) canonical nodes.

questions.prompt: A Fenwick tree steps by the lowest set bit. What is `6 & -6`?
questions.explanation: 6 is 110 in binary; its lowest set bit is 10, which is 2.

questions.prompt: Write `count_components(n, edges)` that returns the number of connected components of an undirected graph on vertices `0..n-1` with the given edge list (pairs), using union-find or any method.
questions.explanation: Each successful union merges two components, reducing the count by one.

questions.prompt: In KMP, what does `lps[i]` store?
choices: The length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix of it
The index of the first mismatch
The number of occurrences of P[i] in P
questions.answer: The length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix of it
questions.explanation: This self-overlap tells KMP how far to fall back after a mismatch.

questions.prompt: Rabin-Karp can take Θ(nm) time in the worst case because of hash collisions.
questions.explanation: If many windows collide with the pattern's hash, each needs an O(m) character check.

questions.prompt: Write `lps(pattern)` that returns the KMP failure array: `lps[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix of it.
questions.explanation: Extend the current border when characters match, otherwise fall back through earlier borders.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems is NP-complete?
questions.explanation: 3-SAT is a classic NP-complete problem; the others have polynomial-time algorithms.

questions.prompt: Explain what it means for a problem to be NP-complete and how a polynomial-time reduction is used to show it.
rubric: States the problem is in NP
States every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time (NP-hard)
Explains that reducing a known NP-complete problem to it proves hardness
Notes a polynomial algorithm would give P = NP
questions.model: A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. To show a new problem is NP-complete, reduce a known NP-complete problem to it in polynomial time and show it is in NP. A polynomial algorithm for any NP-complete problem would imply P = NP.
questions.explanation: Membership in NP plus NP-hardness defines NP-completeness; reductions transfer hardness.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: B is at least as hard as A
Take both endpoints of a maximal matching
questions.explanation: Each pair names a core idea from the unit.
